subject: physics

unit.name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
question_text: When 100 J of work is done on a flywheel, its angular velocity increases from 60 rpm to 180 rpm. What is the moment of inertia of the wheel?

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 7 SHORT ANSWER 11 (numerical; the book prints the answer 0.63 kg·m²). The split is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher. Arithmetic hand-checked: ω₁ = 2π, ω₂ = 6π; 100 = ½I(36π² − 4π²) = 16π²I → I = 6.25/π² ≈ 0.63 kg·m².

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The two ω values
steps.margin_note: Same 2π/60 conversion as every flywheel problem — done twice.
steps.why: Keeping both in terms of π makes the squares subtract cleanly in the next step; converting to decimals early invites rounding error.
common_mistakes: Converting one speed and not the other.

steps.label: Work-energy theorem
lines: The work done equals the change in
steps.margin_note: This is Unit 6’s work-energy theorem wearing rotational clothes — say the connection.
steps.why: The same theorem proved in Work Power Energy, with ½Iω² standing in for ½mv². Cross-chapter links like this are what the examiners reward.
common_mistakes: Writing W = ½I(ω₂ − ω₁)² — the SQUARES are differenced, not the difference squared.

recall.must_convey: That the work equals the change in rotational kinetic energy, W = ½I(ω₂² − ω₁²).
accept: work is change in rotational kinetic energy
half I omega two squared minus half I omega one squared

steps.label: The value
steps.margin_note: One substitution line, one boxed value with its unit — kg·m², the unit of moment of inertia.
steps.why: 36π² − 4π² = 32π², halved is 16π². Keeping π symbolic to the last line is what makes the arithmetic this short.
common_mistakes: Unit slip: writing kg·m/s² (a force unit) instead of kg·m².
